description: Inbound relative-path validation corpus (REQ-T11). A sender is untrusted even when paired: pairing proves who is sending, not that what they send is well-formed. One malformed path escaping the destination directory turns a file-transfer app into an arbitrary-file-write primitive. See ProjectInfo/04-PROTOCOL.md section 8.
derivation: Enumerated from the section 8 rule list, one case per rule plus the ordering cases. Reason names are the canonical protocol names.
checkOrderNote: The order of checks is normative because it decides which reason a path violating several rules is reported under. The order is: empty, length, NUL, surrogate, backslash, UNC, absolute, drive letter, segment count, then per-segment (empty, traversal, current-dir, control char, forbidden char, trailing dot/space, reserved name). The ordering cases below exist to pin it.
failureModeNote: Validation returns a typed result and never throws. A single bad path must fail one item, not the whole transfer: the caller emits itemResult{ok:false, error:'PATH_REJECTED'} and continues. An implementation that throws would abort a 2000-file folder because one file had an awkward name.
normalisationNote: Unicode normalisation is deliberately NOT applied. Normalising rewrites the path and breaks the correspondence between the hash the sender computed and the filename the receiver writes.

accept.note: interior spaces are fine; only trailing ones are not
only a trailing dot is a hazard
not a reserved name; only the exact stems CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9 are
stem is 'null' which is NOT reserved; the reserved stem is exactly 'nul'
decomposed e + combining acute must pass through unchanged, not be folded to U+00E9

reject.note: doubled separator normalises differently per platform
reserved with or without an extension
reserved in any directory, not only the root
Windows strips it, so 'evil.' and 'evil' become the same file
a NUL truncates the path in any C-based syscall layer, so a naive check passes and a different file opens

generatedRejects.name: unpaired high surrogate
generatedRejects.note: Expressed as a generator rather than a literal because a lone surrogate cannot be carried in a JSON string: strict parsers reject it. That limitation is itself the reason the rule exists — unpaired surrogates survive in a UTF-16 string but corrupt on encode, and filesystems normalise them inconsistently, which breaks the hash-to-filename correspondence.

orderingVectors.name: UNC beats ABSOLUTE
orderingVectors.note: '//x' is both UNC-shaped and absolute-shaped. The UNC diagnosis is the more specific one, so the two-slash form is checked first.

orderingVectors.name: BACKSLASH beats DRIVE_LETTER
orderingVectors.note: The backslash check precedes the drive-letter check, so a classic Windows absolute path reports BACKSLASH. Both reject it; only the reported reason differs, and implementations must agree on which.

orderingVectors.name: CONTAINS_NUL beats TRAVERSAL
orderingVectors.note: The NUL check runs before any segment splitting.

orderingVectors.name: BACKSLASH beats TRAVERSAL
orderingVectors.note: Separator validation precedes segment analysis, because segment analysis is only meaningful once the separator is known to be '/'.

orderingVectors.name: ALTERNATE_DATA_STREAM beats FORBIDDEN_CHARACTER for ':'
orderingVectors.note: ':' is in the forbidden set, but the stream-marker diagnosis is more specific.

sanitizeOutgoingVectors.note: the separator is replaced, not treated as structure
prefixed rather than renamed, so the original is still readable
trims to empty, then falls back

notes: The rules are deliberately stricter than either OS requires. Veyro validates against the union of POSIX and Windows hazards regardless of which platform receives, because a file received on Android may later sync to Windows, and a name that is merely awkward on one platform is a vulnerability on the other.
sanitizeOutgoing is for names WE produce. Never apply it to received input: silently rewriting a hostile path hides an attack instead of failing it.
A rejected path fails one item. The transfer continues with the next.
After validation the resolved absolute target must still be inside the destination directory. That check is the caller's and is not covered by this corpus.
